summary: Describes an ATM package for the Media Gateway Control Protocol, adding new connection options, ATM-specific events and signals, connection parameters, and a description of codec and profile negotiation. It extends MGCP as deployed in products at the time and notes the Megaco work.

eli5.summary: MGCP controls phone-call gateways. This note adds extra instructions so the same controller can handle gateways that carry calls over ATM networks.

questions: media gateway atm events and signals
subtitle: Extensions to MGCP for controlling voice gateways connected to ATM networks.

tldr.problem: The Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) is designed to control voice gateways that convert between circuit-switched telephony networks and IP or other media. While MGCP was originally IP-centric, some media gateways connect to Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) networks, which use different technical parameters and procedures than IP networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines an ATM package for MGCP: a modular set of ATM-specific connection options (settings for how ATM bearer connections are set up and configured), signals (notifications of events), events (things that can happen on an ATM connection), and parameters (like codec profiles). Controllers can use these options to tell ATM-based media gateways how to set up calls.
tldr.outcome: A controller can now manage voice gateways connected to both IP networks and ATM networks using MGCP, with ATM-specific configuration that accounts for ATM adaptation layers, virtual circuits, and codec profiles.

today: RFC 3441 is an Informational document describing ATM extensions to MGCP as deployed in products in the early 2000s. It has not been updated or obsoleted. However, MGCP and ATM-based carrier networks have largely given way to SIP and IP-based VoIP architectures. The document remains useful for legacy implementations and historical reference, but new voice gateway deployments typically use SIP or Megaco (H.248) instead of MGCP.

sections.title: MGCP and Media Gateways
sections.content:
The Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) is a protocol for controlling voice and media gateways from a call control element (a central controller). A media gateway sits at the boundary between different networks: it receives voice calls from one network (circuit-switched telephony, ATM, IP, or a mix) and forwards them to another. MGCP lets a controller in a call center or carrier network tell the gateway which calls to route where and how to handle them.

Most MGCP specifications assume IP as the underlying bearer—the medium carrying the voice packets. However, some deployments use ATM as the bearer. ATM is a cell-based packet switching protocol used in carriers' backbone networks and in some older telephony systems. When voice travels over ATM, the technical details are very different from IP: ATM uses adaptation layers to convert voice into cells, virtual circuits to define paths, and different codecs and signaling.

This RFC adds an ATM package to MGCP: a modular extension that controllers can use to configure gateways connected to ATM networks. The package includes connection options (parameters for setting up ATM connections), signals and events (specific to ATM), and codec profiles. The package is optional; gateways that only handle IP do not need to support it.
sections.eli5: MGCP is a remote control for phone gateways. This RFC adds ATM-specific buttons so the remote control can talk to gateways connected to ATM phone networks.

sections.title: ATM Bearer Connections and Adaptation Layers
sections.content:
ATM works by breaking voice or data into fixed-size cells (53 bytes) that travel across virtual circuits. A virtual circuit is a logical path through an ATM network. It can be a permanent virtual circuit (PVC)—provisioned in advance like a leased line—or a switched virtual circuit (SVC)—set up on demand using signaling, similar to a phone call.

Voice does not naturally fit into ATM cells; you need an adaptation layer to convert between continuous voice streams and cells. The RFC supports several ATM Adaptation Layers (AALs). AAL1 is for constant-bit-rate services like structured voice (T1/E1 trunks digitized at fixed rates). AAL2 is for variable-bit-rate voice and data. AAL5 is for packet data. Each requires different configuration.

A Connection Element Identifier (ci) parameter identifies which virtual circuit or sub-channel to use. It can reference a VC by its virtual path and channel numbers, by an ATM address (E.164 phone number, NSAP address, or gateway alias), or by a Bearer Connection Group (a bundle of related VCs).
sections.eli5: ATM sends voice in cells along numbered pipelines. The RFC lets you tell a gateway which pipeline to use, whether it is a standing connection or demand-set, and what format the voice should be in.

sections.title: Connection Options and Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC defines five categories of Local Connection Options (LCOs)—settings the controller can send when creating or modifying a connection.

ATM Bearer Connection options specify the type of ATM connection: the adaptation layer, whether it is a PVC or SVC, whether path setup signaling is enabled, and the connection element identifier (which VC or sub-channel to use).

ATM Adaptation Layer options fine-tune the chosen adaptation layer. For AAL1, you specify partial fill (how many payload octets per cell), clock recovery type (for unstructured data), and whether forward error correction is enabled. For AAL2, you can specify a list of profiles (different codec and service combinations), whether to use simplified CPS (one packet per cell), and various service access points and circuit/frame mode settings.

Service Layer options specify the voice codecs (like G.729, PCMU), their packet lengths, and packetization intervals. Separate options exist for voice (vsel), data (dsel), and fax (fsel), allowing different services to use different codecs on the same connection. You can also specify codec configuration details (vendor-specific bit-maps) and ISUP user information for signaling interoperability.

ATM Bearer Traffic Management options configure how ATM cells are scheduled and prioritized on the link. AAL Dimensioning options specify buffer sizes and resource allocation for the adaptation layer.

When a controller audits (queries) a gateway for capabilities, the gateway reports which options and values it supports, letting the controller choose compatible settings for new connections.
sections.eli5: The RFC defines dozens of dials and knobs: which ATM pipeline, which codec, how fast, whether to recover from errors, whether to bundle multiple calls. The controller sends these settings, and the gateway applies them.

sections.title: Codec Profiles and Negotiation
sections.content:
In ATM voice services, a profile is a predefined set of codec choices and parameters. Different vendors and standards bodies (ITU, ATM Forum, Cisco, etc.) define profiles. An ATM gateway might support multiple profiles. A profile list (pfl) LCO lets the controller specify, in order of preference, which profiles the gateway should use on a connection.

Profiles are identified by type and number. The type indicates the source: AAL2/ITU (ITU-defined), AAL2/ATMF (ATM Forum), AAL2/custom (vendor-defined), or AAL2/Cisco, AAL2/IEEE:00000C (vendor-specific by corporate name or IEEE OUI).

When the controller wants to negotiate which codec to use, it specifies the preferred profile and then uses codec selection options (vsel, dsel, fsel) to indicate which rows in that profile's table should be used for voice, data, and fax. Different rows may use different codecs or rates. This allows a single connection to support multiple service types negotiated from a single profile table.

The RFC provides guidelines for consistency: the chosen codec must be available in the chosen profile, and codec selection must be compatible with the adaptation layer and AAL options.
sections.eli5: Think of profiles like menus at a restaurant: each menu lists available dishes. The controller picks a menu (profile) and then points to which dishes (codecs) to use for different purposes (voice, fax, data).

sections.title: Status and Relationship to Other Standards
sections.content:
This RFC documents ATM package specifications for MGCP as deployed in products in the early 2000s. The document is Informational, not standards-track, and comes with a note that implementers should be aware of developments in the IETF Megaco Working Group and ITU Study Group 16, which were working on potential successors to MGCP.

The package is modular: gateways supporting ATM use the atm/ prefix for all ATM-specific options and events. A gateway can also support other packages (for IP, CAS-based circuit switching, etc.) in the same device. The package specification defines version 0 of the ATM package; future versions could extend it.

The RFC reflects the reality of ATM-based voice networks as they existed in carriers' networks at the time. While ATM has largely been superseded by IP-based carrier networks and VoIP, the specifications remain useful for implementations that continue to use ATM.
sections.eli5: This document describes how real phone gateways at the time controlled ATM voice calls. It is informational—it documents what was done, not a strict standard. Better, more modern standards may follow.
